<reason>Side B (PRO) won a closely fought debate by consistently converting Side A's own material into liabilities. The sickle-cell comparator was boomeranged into a cost argument for MRT; the IVF precedent was turned against CON's "genetic relatedness is a mere preference" claim (public systems already fund IVF for relatedness), a reversal CON asserted away but never closed — CON's closing claim that PRO "never answered" what public money buys misdescribes the exchange. PRO answered both pressure questions directly and cleanly (program cost via existing infrastructure; system ownership via the "identical liability" point), while CON's threshold answer, though defensible via the IVF path, stayed vague under double pressure. PRO's motion-text rebuttal ("to prevent severe inherited mitochondrial disease" contains the restriction CON called smuggling) defused the late framing charge. CON's strongest assets — the non-identity argument that MRT treats no existing patient, and the license-versus-formulary distinction — were original and genuinely damaging, keeping this competitive, but PRO's equity framing and cleaner clash resolution gave the surer path to a vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was PRO's [B2.7]/[B5.4] reversal of CON's "preference, not health" argument: since public systems already fund IVF precisely to secure genetically related children, CON's stated principle for refusing MRT applies to funded care CON implicitly accepts — and CON never explained why the principle stops at MRT.</best_rebuttal>
